newsitem.title: USA: Clinton critic pushes impeachment proceedings.
newsitem.headline: Clinton critic pushes impeachment proceedings.

text.p: A Republican member of the House Judiciary Committee said Wednesday he believes there is enough evidence to begin an impeachment inquiry against President Clinton and Vice President Al Gore.
Representative Bob Barr told a forum sponsored by the conservative weekly newspaper Human Events "I think there is very clear evidence that crimes have indeed been committed."
"I think it is high time for the House of Representatives, which is the only mechanism in our government that has the power to do this, to begin to look at the process," he said.
So far, the Georgia Republican is a lone public voice in Congress urging an impeachment inquiry in connection with the campaign funds issue.

Judiciary Committee Chairman Henry Hyde, an Illinois Republican, said in response to a request by Barr last month that he would study impeachment if federal and congressional investigations of illegal foreign donations to Democrats and other improper activities uncover "a smoking gun."

Barr said Wednesday Attorney General Janet Reno's decision not to call for an independent counsel to investigate the fund-raising abuses dogging Clinton's White House and the Democratic Party was reason for the Judiciary Committee to initiate impeachment proceedings.
Her decision "is ample proof that the Clinton administration is completely unable or unwilling to police itself," said Barr, a former federal prosecutor.

Under the Constitution, the House takes the first step toward initiating impeachment. Should an inquiry get under way, the committee would consider and vote on articles of impeachment -- similar to indictments in a court proceeding -- and, if adopted, the full House would then consider them.

If the House voted to impeach, the Senate would act as a jury to weigh removal from office on grounds of treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors. The Constitution dictates that only the Senate can remove a president or vice president or federal judge from office.
C. Boyden Gray, former President George Bush's White House counsel, also attacked Reno's decision.

Among the arguments for an independent counsel raised by Gray and others were telephone calls made by Gore from the White House to solicit money, which critics contend violated laws against seeking donations in federal offices. Gore said he did not use tax money but used a campaign credit card.
Clinton has said he cannot recall whether he made telephone calls from the White House although Democratic Party documents suggest he was asked to make telephone calls.
